title: The 5PM Survival Guide: How to Handle the ‘Witching Hour’ Without Handing Over an iPad
author: Katherine Martinko
summary: Katherine Martinko describes the familiar 5 PM collapse, when a tired parent has dinner to make and children are bickering and asking for the iPad. She presents a low-energy evening protocol of twenty low-prep, independent activities for children aged two to ten that can become go-to substitutes for a screen. She begins by normalising the parent's depleted bandwidth, calling it valid rather than a moral failure, and then argues that preparation is what makes the difference. Her advice is to keep a mental list of ideas, stock simple materials, and keep devices out of sight so they do not undermine redirection. The activities pair tactile play with audio, use the kitchen and household items, and include chores framed as games, large-format drawing, sensory bins, and a bath before dinner. The piece reads as a practical companion to her broader case against screen-based childhood.
points: Martinko begins by removing guilt, saying that having no emotional bandwidth at 5 PM is normal and not a character flaw.
Her central strategy is advance preparation: a mental menu of ideas and a stock of materials that a child can start without help.
Keeping devices out of view matters because seeing them undermines attempts to redirect play.
Pairing a screen-free audio source such as an audiobook with a hands-on activity such as LEGO or play dough is a recurring formula.
Many suggestions use ordinary household things such as sinks, boxes, cookie dough, and painter's tape, so no purchases or setup are needed.
quotes: Please know that the idea of having no remaining emotional or mental bandwidth is completely valid, and not a sign of moral failure.

Preparation helps, however. Anything you can do ahead of time to take the pressure off that 5PM crunch is worthwhile, even if it’s just coming up with a mental list of possible activities that you can suggest to an aimless child or collecting materials and supplies for independent play.
Be sure to put devices away from view, too, as seeing them can undermine your efforts to redirect their play.
Any kind of screen-free listening device, paired with a tactile activity, is a smart strategy.
It might seem counterintuitive to add energy to an already-overwhelming situation, but music and dance have a remarkable ability to defuse stress and leave everyone feeling better.
Get them cleaning. Young kids are curiously willing to pitch in with chores.
There is novelty in scale; for some reason, this is much more exciting for kids than drawing on regular-size paper.
